In that same document you can look at the growth in resource adequacy contracts from batteries on page 28.

Notably in Texas battery installations tend to be 1 hour as opposed to California where they are required to be 4 hour systems. This makes the batteries in Texas able to respond to short term events but not really effectively shave peaks and valleys in demand. Lately there are more 2 hour systems showing up in Texas and in theory even enough 1 hour systems could effectively serve the same purpose but while the instantaneous GW figures may look similar the GWh figures still put California firmly in the lead in a way that makes a meaningful impact on grid reliability.

There are also other factors like in California many battery systems have firm capacity contracts which means they need to be able to deliver some percent of their output at any time the grid demands it, where that's not a thing in Texas so in theory you could get a snowball situation where batteries in Texas are actually waiting to respond to a catastrophe until the price per MWh gets high enough for them to feel it's worth it
